source: Didolkar et al. (2024) Metacognitive Capabilities of LLMs: An Exploration in Mathematical Problem Solving
finding: Declarative metacognitive knowledge made explicit: GPT-4 labels each training question with a fine-grained skill, then clusters the labels into a small skill catalog. This is a model-built class record.
numbers: MATH: about 5000 raw skills reduced to 117 coarse skills; GSM8K: 22 skills. Labelling by GPT-4-0613.
limits: Skills named by one strong model; labels are model-perceived, not checked against human skill taxonomies.
agent_relevance: Template for our class record: let the model name problem classes, cluster them, keep a small catalog.

source: Didolkar et al. (2024) Metacognitive Capabilities of LLMs: An Exploration in Mathematical Problem Solving
finding: Conditional knowledge (which skill applies to this question) used to pick in-context examples. Skill-matched examples beat fixed CoT, random, topic-based and complexity-based examples.
numbers: MATH with GPT-4 CoT: +11.6 points over standard CoT, +3.5 over Complex CoT, +3.5 over topic-based examples. Program-aided: +7.52 over PAL on a 500-problem MATH subset.
limits: Gains depend on label quality; GPT-4 labels gave the best results versus GPT-3.5 and Mixtral labels. Single paper, math only.
agent_relevance: Class label as a retrieval key is worth several points. Supports choosing by class, but the label must be right.

source: Didolkar et al. (2024) Metacognitive Capabilities of LLMs: An Exploration in Mathematical Problem Solving
finding: Skill labels from a strong model transfer to a weaker model and to other datasets (GSM8K skills applied to SVAMP, ASDiv, MAWPS).
numbers: Transfer tested on Mixtral 8x7B using the MATH repository labelled by GPT-4; per-dataset deltas not recorded here.
limits: Math word problems only.
agent_relevance: A class catalog built by a strong model can be reused by a cheaper model: build once, store.

source: Didolkar et al. (2024) Metacognitive Capabilities of LLMs: An Exploration in Mathematical Problem Solving
finding: Weak spot: the label is a topic-like skill, not a strategy. The model is asked what the problem needs, not whether a strategy would fail.
numbers: Two-stage pipeline: label and cluster, then retrieve exemplars by skill for the test question.
limits: No test that the model knows when a skill fails.
agent_relevance: The model only fills a label slot and code does the retrieval, which fits our rule that code decides.

source: Wang & Zhao (2024) Metacognitive Prompting Improves Understanding in Large Language Models
finding: Metacognitive Prompting (MP): five fixed stages (interpret, first judgment, critique, final decision with explanation, confidence). It beat CoT and Plan-and-Solve on ten NLU datasets with four models.
numbers: Zero-shot averages: MP beats CoT by 4.8 to 6.4 points and PS by 2.8 to 4.1. GPT-4 zero-shot first dataset: MP 89.9/86.2 vs CoT 88.9/84.7; largest-gain column MP 64.0 vs CoT 54.7. 5-shot M-MP beats M-CoT by 4.5 to 6.0 and CoT-SC by 2.2 to 3.5.
limits: Understanding tasks (GLUE, SuperGLUE, BLUE, LexGLUE), not reasoning. Stages are applied always, not on a signal.
agent_relevance: Scheduled self-critique helps NLU a little. Our guardrail G1 says doubt only on signal, so this tells us gain size, not a design to copy.

source: Wang & Zhao (2024) Metacognitive Prompting Improves Understanding in Large Language Models
finding: Error analysis of MP: most failures are overthinking, then overcorrection (model flips a right first answer).
numbers: Overthinking 68.3% of MP errors, overcorrection 31.7%. Confidence check: confident and correct 55.6%, confident and wrong 32.5%, unsure and wrong 6.8%, unsure and right 5.1%.
limits: Self-reported confidence only; 32.5% of cases are confidently wrong.
agent_relevance: Models revise right answers when told to reflect, matching our word-puzzle result (92% plain vs 75% with forced doubt). Self-confidence is a weak gate.

source: Kadavath et al. (2022) Language Models (Mostly) Know What They Know
finding: Declarative self-knowledge in LLMs: models can score their own samples with P(True) and predict P(IK), the chance they know the answer, with no proposed answer given.
numbers: Abstract-level findings: P(True) is well calibrated on diverse tasks and improves with scale; self-evaluation improves when the model sees many of its own samples; P(IK) is predicted well after training.
quote: Models perform well at predicting P(IK) and partially generalize across tasks, though they struggle with calibration of P(IK) on new tasks.
limits: P(IK) is trained, not zero-shot, and calibration is poor on new tasks. 2022 models, up to 52B. Only abstract and section list read closely.
agent_relevance: Self-knowledge exists but is task-specific. Prefer measured pass rates per class over asking the model.

source: Kadavath et al. (2022) Language Models (Mostly) Know What They Know
finding: P(IK) responds to context: it rises when relevant source text is in context and with hints toward GSM8K solutions. A form of conditional knowledge (when do I know).
numbers: Qualitative rise in P(IK) with source material and with hints (sections 5.3 and 5.4).
limits: Specific tasks only (trivia-style, GSM8K).
agent_relevance: Supports a pre-attempt check: do I have the needed facts in context.

source: Binder et al. (2024) Looking Inward: Language Models Can Learn About Themselves by Introspection
finding: Self-prediction test: a model finetuned to predict its own behavior in hypothetical scenarios beats a different model trained on its ground-truth behavior.
numbers: GPT-4o: self-prediction advantage of M1 over M2 is +17% accuracy. One reported training result: average accuracy rises from 32.6% to 49.4%.
quote: However, while we successfully elicit introspection on simple tasks, we are unsuccessful on more complex tasks or those requiring out-of-distribution generalization.
limits: Works on simple tasks only; fails on more complex tasks and out-of-distribution generalization (authors' own words).
agent_relevance: Models have limited privileged access to their own tendencies. Do not trust a model's account of which strategy it would use; log what it did.

source: Zhou et al. (2024) Self-Discover: Large Language Models Self-Compose Reasoning Structures
finding: Procedural and conditional knowledge in one loop: the model selects atomic reasoning modules for a task, adapts them, and implements a task-level reasoning structure it then follows on every instance.
numbers: Zero-shot accuracy, PaLM 2-L: BBH 56 direct, 60 CoT, 67 Self-Discover; T4D 30, 40, 69; MATH 45, 42, 50.5. GPT-4: BBH 58, 75, 81; T4D 51, 52, 85; MATH 70.5, 71, 73.
limits: Gains largest on world-knowledge and agent tasks, small on MATH. In MATH error analysis 74.7% of failures were calculation errors, not wrong structure. Same-lab authors.
agent_relevance: Choosing a strategy once per task class, not per call, is cheap and effective. A case for class-level operator choice.

source: Zhou et al. (2024) Self-Discover: Large Language Models Self-Compose Reasoning Structures
finding: Self-Discover is cheaper than sampling methods and the structures transfer across models.
numbers: Beats CoT-Self-Consistency by more than 20 points on some tasks with 10 to 40 times fewer inference calls; up to 32% over CoT; structures from PaLM 2-L work on GPT-4, and from GPT-4 on Llama2.
limits: Per-task, not per-instance; selection uses 3 meta-prompts, no labels.
agent_relevance: Cached task-level structure supports a class record that is reused instead of re-derived.

source: Zhang et al. (2025) Reasoning Strategies in Large Language Models: Can They Follow, Prefer, and Optimize?
finding: Direct test of conditional strategy knowledge: four named deduction strategies prompted on TruthQuest and ZebraLogic. No single strategy beat the no-strategy prompt; an oracle picking the best strategy per problem is far above any fixed one.
numbers: TruthQuest Phi-4: no strategy 47.2%, best single 49.0%, oracle 82.9%. R1-Distill: 63.4% vs oracle 90.1%. ZebraLogic Phi-4: 27.3% vs oracle 37.7%; Qwen3: 32.0% vs oracle 36.4%. Gap up to about 40 points.
limits: Two logic-puzzle datasets, small and mid models. The oracle uses the answer key.
agent_relevance: Headroom for per-class operator choice is large, but only if the choice is correct. The class record should aim at this gap.

source: Zhang et al. (2025) Reasoning Strategies in Large Language Models: Can They Follow, Prefer, and Optimize?
finding: Combining strategies by code beats any single strategy but stays well under the oracle. Model-side selection was not shown to work.
numbers: Phi-4 TruthQuest: best single 49.0%, majority vote 54.9%, verifier 46.9%, vote+prob 57.3%, vote+verifier 55.8%, oracle 82.9%. R1-Distill: verifier 74.1% vs 63.4%. ZebraLogic gains only about 0.6 to 1.1 points.
limits: Gains vary by model and dataset. Strategy outputs from one model are correlated (our G4).
agent_relevance: Self-selection of strategy is not reliable; ensembles give modest gains. A measured class record is the open alternative.

source: Zhang et al. (2025) Reasoning Strategies in Large Language Models: Can They Follow, Prefer, and Optimize?
finding: Models follow a named strategy on instruction, but with very different fidelity, and have default preferences.
numbers: Strategy adherence table: supposition following 99% for one model vs 88%, 81%, 64% for others; chain construction 61%, 12%, 53%, 11%. Prior work (Mondorf and Plank 2024) saw Zephyr-7B use supposition following in 60% of cases.
limits: Adherence judged by manual review of samples; small models.
agent_relevance: Naming an operator in the prompt does not guarantee it is used. Code must check it was applied.

source: Valiente & Pilly (2025) Competence-Aware AI Agents with Metacognition for Unknown Situations and Environments (MUSE)
finding: An agent loop with learned competence self-assessment guiding strategy selection (world-model and LLM versions). Self-assessment sharpens within a few adaptation episodes.
numbers: ALFWorld novel tasks: AUROC2 0.66 and metacognitive accuracy 60% with no adaptation; 0.93 and 85% after five adaptation episodes. A separate headline run reports 92% metacognitive accuracy.
limits: Simulated household tasks; one lab; authors built the baselines.
agent_relevance: Closest existing loop to our class record: measured competence per task type steers the strategy.

source: Valiente & Pilly (2025) Competence-Aware AI Agents with Metacognition for Unknown Situations and Environments (MUSE)
finding: Ablation: self-assessment is the active ingredient. MUSE beats ReAct and Reflexion and loses much of the gain when self-assessment is random or inverted.
numbers: Success on novel tasks (no adaptation / after 5 episodes): ReAct 35/35%, Reflexion 45/51%, Reflexion with supervised learning 62/65%, MUSE with lowest self-assessment 59/61%, MUSE with random self-assessment 68/69%, MUSE 84/90%.
limits: ALFWorld only; random-vs-real gap 16 to 21 points.
agent_relevance: Quantifies a calibrated competence signal: about +16 to +21 points over a random one.

source: Valiente & Pilly (2025) Competence-Aware AI Agents with Metacognition for Unknown Situations and Environments (MUSE)
finding: Small LLMs gain much more from the metacognitive loop than from ReAct or Reflexion.
numbers: After five episodes: Mistral-7B-OpenOrca ReAct 23%, Reflexion 27%, MUSE 58%; OpenELM-3B ReAct 4%, Reflexion 9%, MUSE 55%.
limits: Low baselines; one environment.
agent_relevance: The scaffold may matter most for small models, which is our nano-model setting.

source: Griot et al. (2025) Large Language Models lack essential metacognition for reliable medical reasoning (MetaMedQA)
finding: From search summaries only: on MetaMedQA, models with high multiple-choice accuracy rarely recognise their own knowledge limits; unknown-answer items scored worst.
numbers: Reported in snippets: best model (GPT-4o) identified its limits 3.7% of the time; all but three of twelve models scored 0% on the unknown-answer analysis.
limits: Not opened; numbers need checking against the paper.
agent_relevance: Models answer confidently when no right option exists. Our agent needs an external abstain rule, not self-report.

source: Servajean & Servajean (2026) Measuring (some aspects of) the metacognition of AI
finding: Method paper: common AI confidence-AUC measures are confounded with first-order accuracy; the meta-d' and M-ratio framework from psychology separates metacognitive efficiency from task skill. Three LLMs, three tasks.
numbers: GPT-5, DeepSeek-V3.2-Exp, Mistral-Medium-2508. All models showed substantial meta-d' but always suboptimal M-ratio. GPT-5 type 1 sensitivity in task C was 126% and 130% larger than the other two. AUC2 and d' correlated rs = 0.9, p < 0.002.
limits: Perceptual-style forced-choice tasks, not strategy selection; many M-ratio differences between models were practically inconclusive.
agent_relevance: Use M-ratio, not raw AUC, to compare how well our agent's confidence tracks truth across classes.

source: Servajean & Servajean (2026) Measuring (some aspects of) the metacognition of AI
finding: Signal-detection test of regulation: whether models shift decision criterion with risk. GPT-5 shifted clearly across risk setups, the others less.
numbers: GPT-5 was the only model with significantly different criterion c across all risk configurations; c below -0.6 in one setup and above 0.6 in the opposite.
limits: Three models; small task set.
agent_relevance: Models can adapt response bias to stated stakes, so risk can serve as a conditional signal.

source: Didolkar et al. (2025) Metacognitive Reuse: Turning Recurring LLM Reasoning Into Concise Behaviors
finding: Procedural knowledge made reusable: the model reflects on its own traces and writes short named behaviors (name plus instruction) into a handbook supplied in context later.
numbers: Behavior-conditioned inference cuts reasoning tokens by up to 46% at equal or better accuracy. Behavior-guided self-improvement gives up to 10% higher accuracy than naive critique-and-revise.
limits: Math focus; best-case 'up to' numbers; handbook built from the same model's traces.
agent_relevance: Same shape as our class record, but the model writes the entries. We would add a code check before an entry is stored.

source: Zhang et al. (2025) AdaptThink: Reasoning Models Can Learn When to Think
finding: Learned conditional knowledge: a reasoning model trained by RL to choose thinking or no-thinking by problem difficulty. Simple problems do as well or better with no thinking.
numbers: DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B on three math sets: average response length down 53%, accuracy up 2.4%. Per-dataset: length down 50.9%, 63.5%, 44.7% with accuracy up 4.1%, 1.4%, 1.6%.
limits: Needs RL training of distilled models; not prompt-only. Simple fixed NoThinking loses accuracy on hard sets.
agent_relevance: The 'when' knowledge is real: skip effort on easy classes. A class record could do this by code.

source: Liu et al. (2024) SMART: Self-learning Meta-strategy Agent for Reasoning Tasks
finding: Strategy selection learned by RL: an LM picks among CoT, Least-to-Most and Program-of-Thought in one attempt without refinement; selection modelled as an MDP.
numbers: Up to +15 points on GSM8K (relative +35%) in a single pass; refinement accuracy +16. Gemma 7B fine-tuned baseline 68.7% to 71.8% (+3.1). Out-of-domain SVAMP/ASDiv: +2.6/+2.9 (Gemma), -0.8/+1.0 (Mistral), +1.0/+1.0 (Qwen2).
limits: 7B models; out-of-domain gains small and one negative. Trained, not prompted.
agent_relevance: Per-class strategy preference can be learned, but transfer to new classes is thin. Update the class record online.

source: Kargupta et al. (2025) Cognitive Foundations for Reasoning and Their Manifestation in LLMs
finding: Large trace study: 192K traces from 18 models plus 54 human think-aloud traces coded for 28 cognitive elements, including self-awareness (assess own knowledge and task solvability). Models under-use behaviors that predict success.
numbers: Self-awareness in 49% of human traces vs 19% of model traces; abstraction 54% vs 36%. Only 16% of 1.6K reasoning papers study self-awareness. Self-awareness had negative NPMI with success (-0.141) in model traces.
limits: Coding by LLM annotator; ill-structured vs well-structured problems differ; correlation not cause.
agent_relevance: Models hold repertoires but do not deploy them unprompted; supports program-triggered operators.

source: Kargupta et al. (2025) Cognitive Foundations for Reasoning and Their Manifestation in LLMs
finding: Test-time guidance that scaffolds the successful structure improves performance mostly on ill-structured problems, and can also hurt a lot.
numbers: Up to +66.7% (Qwen3-7B on diagnosis), +60.0% (Qwen3-14B on dilemmas); some categories lost over 50% (for example -72.0%). Baseline success: algorithms 62.2%, story problems 78.8%, design 48.0%.
limits: Big swings on small subsets; some cells at 0% accuracy excluded.
agent_relevance: The right scaffold depends on the problem class and a wrong match can cost over 50 points: the strongest argument for a measured class record.

source: Elenjical et al. (2026) Think2: Grounded Metacognitive Reasoning in Large Language Models
finding: Brown's plan-monitor-evaluate cycle as a prompt architecture plus a dual-process MetaController for effort allocation. Forcing the cycle on a model lacking reasoning training hurt arithmetic.
numbers: GSM8K: Ann Brown framework 69.55% vs Standard 80.71% and CoT 77.98%. Self-correction success 50.0% vs 25.0% for CoT in one table (abstract says threefold vs an aggregate baseline). Blinded human preference 84.1% trustworthiness and 84.2% self-awareness over 580 query pairs.
limits: 8B Llama-3 and Qwen-3 only; human preference measures perceived trust, not accuracy.
agent_relevance: Same lesson as MP: universal metacognitive scaffolding costs accuracy on easy tasks; gate by class and signal.

source: Elenjical et al. (2026) Think2: Grounded Metacognitive Reasoning in Large Language Models
finding: Claims many 'metacognitive' benchmarks test low-order skills (remembering, understanding), so gains may reflect verbosity.
numbers: Cites Zhang et al. (2025) on benchmark cognitive depth; no new count.
limits: Secondhand claim.
agent_relevance: Measure class-record gain on held-out items, not on verbosity-sensitive NLU.

source: Hills (2025) Could you be wrong: Debiasing LLMs using a metacognitive prompt
finding: The follow-up prompt 'could you be wrong?' makes LLMs list errors, biases, counter-evidence and alternatives they left out. Qualitative demonstration only.
numbers: No accuracy numbers; questions taken from articles about LLM biases, plus one incomplete-information example.
limits: Anecdotal, no controls, no measured accuracy change.
agent_relevance: Weak evidence; a probe type, not a verified fix.

source: Steyvers et al. (2025) What Large Language Models Know and What People Think They Know
finding: Users overestimate LLM accuracy with default explanations; longer explanations raise user confidence with no accuracy gain. Aligning explanations with model internal confidence narrowed both the calibration gap and the discrimination gap.
numbers: Multiple-choice and short-answer questions; discrimination measured by AUC (0.5 chance, 1 perfect). Exact N and gap sizes not recorded here.
limits: Human trust study, not strategy knowledge.
agent_relevance: Explanation style moves human trust apart from correctness; length-normalise any scoring (our G5).

source: MetaMedQA reanalysis preprint (2026), search snippet
finding: From a search snippet: confidence-correctness discrimination, missing-answer recognition, unknown-answer detection and abstention can dissociate; stronger models discriminate and calibrate better but keep clinical failures.
numbers: No numbers read.
limits: Not opened; lead only.
agent_relevance: Metacognitive knowledge is not one skill. Test each part separately.

source: Zhang et al. (2025) benchmark cognitive depth, EMNLP Findings, search snippet
finding: From a search snippet: popular benchmarks skew toward remembering and understanding, with metacognitive reasoning under-represented.
numbers: No numbers read.
limits: Not opened; secondhand.
agent_relevance: Few benchmarks test strategy knowledge; we need our own class-record test.
